findings.title: Do not pipe an unverified remote script into sh during build
findings.whyItBreaks: `curl -sL https://example.com/install.sh | sh` downloads mutable remote content and runs it as root in the build. There is no pinned version, checksum or signature. Anyone who controls the host, DNS or TLS path, or who changes the script, can run arbitrary code in the image, and builds are not reproducible. The command also hides failures. `-s` suppresses errors and `-f` is absent, so an HTTP 4xx/5xx error page is passed to `sh` as a script. Alpine's `/bin/sh` has no pipefail, so a failed curl leaves `sh` reading empty or partial input. That can exit 0 and let the build succeed with a missing or half-run install, or it can run a truncated script. The placeholder `example.com` URL also means the build currently depends on a host that does not serve a real installer.

findings.title: LoadOrDefault swallows ErrMissing, conflating missing key with empty value
findings.whyItBreaks: Load returns ("", ErrMissing) when the key is absent (src/store.go:7-12). The new exported LoadOrDefault drops that error with `v, _ := Load(...)` and returns a bare string. A missing key and a key legitimately stored as "" both produce "". The function takes no caller-supplied default and has no ok/error return, so no caller can tell failure from a real value. Any caller that persists, bills or reports the result will treat a missing key as real empty data. The "OrDefault" name suggests a configurable default, but the only default is the zero value, which is not distinguishable from valid data.

findings.title: Run returns before results are sent; goroutines leak and ignore ctx
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change, Run sent every result synchronously, so all sends had finished when it returned. A caller could then close(results) or read exactly len(jobs) values. Now each send runs in a detached goroutine and Run returns immediately with no WaitGroup. A caller that closes `results` after Run returns will make the pending goroutines panic with 'send on closed channel'. A caller that ranges over the channel after Run returns sees it end early or never. If the receiver stops reading, for example on ctx cancel, every pending goroutine blocks forever on the send. The goroutines never check ctx, which Run already receives, so they cannot be cancelled. Result order also becomes nondeterministic. The repo has no in-repo callers, but Run is exported and its completion semantics changed.

findings.title: Run returns before results are sent; goroutines leak and ignore ctx

Now each send runs in an untracked goroutine and Run returns immediately. (1) A caller that does `Run(...); close(results)` will panic with 'send on closed channel', or will lose results. (2) A caller that stops reading after Run returns leaves one goroutine blocked forever per job. These goroutines never check ctx.Done(), so cancelling ctx cannot release them. (3) Results now arrive in nondeterministic order, where they used to follow the order of jobs. Run is exported and its signature is unchanged, so existing callers get no signal that the contract changed.

findings.title: Delete permission uses OR, allowing cross-tenant and non-admin deletes
findings.whyItBreaks: The base version required both admin status and a matching tenant. With `||`, any admin can delete records in any tenant (cross-tenant access). Any non-admin user can also delete any record in their own tenant, because only the tenant check has to pass. Both cases are privilege escalation. Substituting values: isAdmin=false with matching tenant returns true, and isAdmin=true with a different tenant returns true. Both were false before.

For `[done, done, pending]`, index 0 is removed, the array becomes `[done, pending]`, and index 1 is `pending`. The remaining done job is never removed and is returned as if pending. The function also now mutates the caller's input array in place, where the old `filter` returned a new array. Any caller that holds the original reference sees it change.

findings.title: TtlCache.get returns only expired entries and deletes fresh ones
findings.whyItBreaks: The comparison was flipped from `< ttlMs` to `> ttlMs`. A fresh entry (age <= ttl) now falls through to `this.entries.delete(key)` and returns null, so a get right after a set always misses and the entry is dropped. An expired entry (age > ttl) is returned as a hit. The cache therefore never serves valid data and serves stale data instead.

findings.title: pruneDone mutates input while iterating and skips adjacent done jobs
findings.whyItBreaks: `splice` inside `forEach` shifts the remaining elements left, but the iteration index still advances. The element that moves into the removed slot is never visited. For `[{done:true},{done:true},{done:false}]`, the second done job is skipped and stays in the result. The function also now mutates the caller's array in place. The previous `filter` version returned a new array and left the input untouched. Any caller that still holds the original array sees it change, and the returned array can still contain done jobs.

findings.title: Restore empty-input guard in averageAmount
findings.whyItBreaks: The removed `if (rows.length === 0) return 0;` was the only handling of empty input. With an empty array, `reduce` returns 0 and the function computes 0/0, which is NaN. The function is typed `number`, so callers cannot see the failure from the type. A NaN can be persisted, serialized (JSON turns it into null) or displayed. Before this change an empty input returned 0.

findings.title: Do not sort the caller's array in place in busiest
findings.whyItBreaks: The old code copied the input with `[...rows]` before sorting. The new `rows.sort(...)` mutates the caller's array and reorders it by descending amount. A function named `busiest` that returns one row gives no hint of this side effect. Any caller that later depends on the original order (display order, index-based lookups, shared or cached arrays) gets silently reordered data. It would also throw on a frozen or readonly array.

findings.title: Restore empty-input guard in averageAmount
findings.whyItBreaks: The removed `if (rows.length === 0) return 0;` guard means an empty array now computes 0 / 0, which is NaN. The function's return type is `number`, so callers get NaN instead of the previous 0. NaN propagates silently into later arithmetic, comparisons and JSON serialization (where it becomes null). The function is exported, so every consumer is affected. This is a behavior regression from the previous contract.

findings.title: Avoid mutating caller's array in busiest
findings.whyItBreaks: The change drops the defensive copy (`[...rows]`) and calls `rows.sort(...)` directly. Array.prototype.sort sorts in place, so `busiest(rows)` now reorders the caller's input array as a side effect. Any caller that reuses `rows` afterwards sees a different order. Examples are display order, index-based logic, or a later `averageAmount` call that doesn't care but a paginator that does. A read-only-looking query function is now mutating, and it throws on frozen or readonly arrays.

findings.title: Restore empty-input guard in averageAmount
findings.whyItBreaks: The `rows.length === 0` early return was removed. For an empty array, `reduce` returns 0 and `0 / 0` gives NaN. The function is declared to return `number` and used to return 0 for empty input. Callers that display, sum or persist the value now get NaN, and the type signature gives no warning.

findings.title: Avoid in-place sort of caller's array in busiest
findings.whyItBreaks: The old code sorted a copy with `[...rows].sort(...)`. The new code calls `rows.sort(...)` on the input, so each call to this exported read-only helper reorders the caller's array by descending amount. Any caller that keeps using the array afterwards, such as a display list or index-based logic, sees the changed order. This is also a data-integrity problem for shared or frozen arrays: a frozen array makes `sort` throw a TypeError.

findings.title: Restore numeric comparator in rankScores sort
findings.whyItBreaks: `Array.prototype.sort()` with no comparator orders elements by their string form (UTF-16 code units), not numerically. `scores.sort(); scores.reverse();` therefore does not produce a descending numeric order. Example: scores [5, 10, 100, 9] sort as strings to [10, 100, 5, 9] and reverse to [9, 5, 100, 10]. With n=1, the cutoff is 9, so topPlayers returns the first player with score >= 9 in input order, which is not necessarily the top scorer. With n=2, the cutoff is 5, so it returns the first two players with score >= 5 (for example 5 and 10) instead of 100 and 10. Negative scores and decimals are also ordered wrongly, because '-' sorts before digits and '.' sorts by character code. topPlayers and formatBoard (which calls it) are the only users of rankScores, and both return wrong leaderboard results.

findings.title: Numeric sort replaced by default lexicographic sort
findings.whyItBreaks: `Array.prototype.sort()` with no comparator orders elements by their string form. For scores [100, 9, 10] it gives ["10","100","9"], and reversing that gives [9, 100, 10] instead of [100, 10, 9]. `topPlayers` uses `scores[min(n, len) - 1]` as the cutoff. With n=1 the cutoff is 9, so the filter keeps every player and `.slice(0, 1)` returns the first player in input order, not the top scorer. Negative scores are also misordered ("-5" sorts before "-10" as a string). The previous code used `(a, b) => b - a`, which was correct. `formatBoard` calls `topPlayers`, so the printed leaderboard is wrong too. Separately, `topPlayers` never sorts the players it returns; it filters by cutoff and keeps input order. That predates this PR and is out of scope.

findings.title: Restore numeric comparator in rankScores sort
findings.whyItBreaks: `Array.prototype.sort()` with no comparator orders elements by their string form, so "10" < "2" < "9". The old code used `(a, b) => b - a`. Take scores [9, 10, 2] and n=1. `sort()` gives [10, 2, 9] and `reverse()` gives [9, 2, 10]. The cutoff is then scores[0] = 9 instead of 10. `players.filter(score >= 9).slice(0, 1)` returns the first matching player in input order, which is the 9-point player, not the top scorer. Negative scores also sort wrongly ("-1" sorts after "-10"). `formatBoard` at line 20 calls `topPlayers`, so the displayed leaderboard is wrong too.

findings.title: Use constant-time comparison for webhook signature verification
findings.whyItBreaks: `verify` replaced `hmac.compare_digest(expected, given_signature)` with `signature_of(...) == given_signature`. Python's `==` on strings short-circuits at the first differing character, so response time leaks how many leading characters of the guessed signature are correct. An attacker who can send repeated requests to `handle` (the 401/200 gate) can recover a valid HMAC for an arbitrary payload byte by byte and forge webhooks that reach `processor(payload)`. `handle` at app/webhook.py:14 is the sole caller and fully trusts this result for authentication.

findings.title: Use constant-time comparison for webhook HMAC verification
findings.whyItBreaks: `verify` used `hmac.compare_digest` and now uses `==` on the expected HMAC hex digest and the attacker-supplied `given_signature`. String `==` returns at the first differing character, so response timing leaks how many leading characters of the signature are correct. An attacker can use that to forge a valid signature for an arbitrary payload one character at a time and bypass webhook authentication. `handle` (app/webhook.py:14) relies on `verify` as its only auth gate before running `processor(payload)`. A second effect of the change: `hmac.compare_digest` raises TypeError if a str argument contains non-ASCII characters, whereas `==` does not. Neither behavior is the reason to revert, but the constant-time comparison is the established safe primitive here.

findings.title: Use constant-time comparison for webhook HMAC signature
findings.whyItBreaks: `signature_of(...) == given_signature` is a short-circuiting string comparison. Response time depends on how many leading characters of the attacker-supplied signature match the real HMAC. An attacker who can send repeated requests to `handle` can recover a valid signature byte by byte and forge webhook payloads that pass `verify` and reach `processor`. The previous `hmac.compare_digest` was constant-time and prevented this. `verify` is the only authentication gate in `handle` (app/webhook.py:14).

findings.title: Balance updates moved outside the transaction block
findings.whyItBreaks: Before the change, the ledger INSERT and both balance UPDATEs ran inside one `with db.transaction():` block, so they committed or rolled back together. Now only `_record_ledger` is inside the `with`, and `_apply_balances` is dedented to run after the block exits. The ledger row is committed first. If the debit or credit then raises (a constraint violation, a lost connection, or a crash between the two UPDATEs), the ledger records a transfer that never moved money. A failure between the two UPDATEs debits the source without crediting the destination, which loses money. The two balance UPDATEs also now run outside any transaction, so they are not atomic with each other.

findings.title: Balance updates run outside the transaction, breaking transfer atomicity
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change the ledger INSERT and both balance UPDATEs ran in one `with db.transaction():` block. Now only `_record_ledger` is inside the block, and `_apply_balances` at line 24 is dedented, so it runs after the transaction commits. If the debit succeeds and the credit fails (constraint error, a missing destination account, a connection drop, a crash between statements), the ledger row is already committed and the money is half-moved or lost. The two UPDATEs are also not atomic with each other. A ledger entry can exist with no balance change, or a debit can exist with no credit. This is a data-integrity regression on a money path.

findings.title: Balance updates run outside the transaction block
findings.whyItBreaks: Only `_record_ledger` is inside `with db.transaction():`. `_apply_balances` is dedented to line 24, so it runs after the transaction commits. If the debit or credit raises (constraint violation, missing account, connection drop, crash between the two UPDATEs), the ledger INSERT is already committed. The result is a ledger entry with no balance change, or a debit with no matching credit. That is permanent money-inconsistency data corruption. The previous code did the INSERT and both UPDATEs in one atomic transaction. The two UPDATEs are also no longer atomic with each other. Unless the db object autocommits, they also run in whatever implicit transaction state the connection is in.

findings.title: billingDay switched from UTC to host-local timezone
findings.whyItBreaks: The base used getUTCFullYear/getUTCMonth/getUTCDate, so a given instant always mapped to one deterministic billing day. The new code uses getFullYear/getMonth/getDate, which read the process's local timezone. For example, 2026-11-21T23:30:00Z gives 2026-11-21 on a UTC host but 2026-11-22 on a UTC+2 host, and 2026-11-20 on a UTC-5 host. Billing-day boundaries therefore move with the deployment's TZ, or with a developer machine's TZ. Usage can be bucketed into the wrong day or invoice period. Day keys can also differ from previously persisted UTC-based keys after an upgrade or a host move. sameBillingDay (line 8) inherits the same behavior. The function is exported, and nothing in the diff or repo indicates the move to local time is intentional.

findings.whyItBreaks: The base version used getUTCFullYear/getUTCMonth/getUTCDate. The new code uses getFullYear/getMonth/getDate, which read the process's local timezone. The same instant now maps to a different billing day depending on the TZ of the host. For example, 2026-11-21T23:30:00Z is 2026-11-21 in UTC but 2026-11-22 at UTC+8. Usage near midnight UTC is assigned to a different day than before. Results also differ between hosts and CI, and daily billing boundaries and sameBillingDay comparisons shift without anyone intending it. The change looks like a pure refactor, and nothing in the diff or repo suggests local time was intended. The repo contains no other references to UTC or timezone handling.

findings.whyItBreaks: The base implementation used getUTCFullYear/getUTCMonth/getUTCDate, so a given instant always mapped to one deterministic billing day. The new code uses getFullYear/getMonth/getDate, which read the process's local timezone. For example, 2026-11-21T20:00:00Z returns 2026-11-21 on a UTC host but 2026-11-22 on a UTC+8 host. Billing days therefore change with deployment TZ or TZ env, and the same instant can land in different days across machines. findings.title: Include tenant in profile cache key to prevent cross-tenant leak
findings.whyItBreaks: readProfile(tenant, account, fetchProfile) fetches by (tenant, account), and Profile carries a tenant field. The memo key is now just `account`. If tenant A reads account 'alice', the profile is cached under 'alice'. A later readProfile('B', 'alice', ...) hits the cache and returns tenant A's profile without calling fetchProfile. That returns the wrong data and leaks it across tenants. Account ids are normally unique only within a tenant, so collisions are realistic. The old key `${tenant}:${account}` prevented this.

findings.title: Include tenant in profile memo key to prevent cross-tenant leakage
findings.whyItBreaks: The memo key was `${tenant}:${account}` and is now just `account`. `readProfile` takes `tenant` and passes it to `fetchProfile`, and `Profile` carries a `tenant` field, so the same account ID can exist in several tenants. Substituting values: `readProfile('A','bob',f)` caches under `'bob'`. A later `readProfile('B','bob',f)` hits `memo.get('bob')`, finds the entry, and returns tenant A's profile without calling `fetchProfile`. The caller gets another tenant's data (`displayName`, `tenant`). That is a cross-tenant data leak and a wrong result. The memo is module-global and never evicted, so it persists for the life of the process.

findings.title: Include tenant in profile cache key to prevent cross-tenant leakage
findings.whyItBreaks: The module-level `memo` is shared by all callers. The key changed from `${tenant}:${account}` to just `account`, but `fetchProfile` is still called with `(tenant, account)` and the Profile includes `tenant`. If tenant A reads account 'alice' and then tenant B reads account 'alice', B hits the cache and gets A's Profile, including A's tenant and displayName. B's fetch never runs. That is a cross-tenant data leak and wrong data. Account ids are commonly unique only within a tenant, which is why the old key included the tenant.

findings.title: load() swallows missing-key error and returns empty string
findings.whyItBreaks: The `throw new Error(`missing: ${key}`)` is now caught by the new catch-all in the same function, which returns "". Before this change a missing key raised an error. Now a missing key gives the same result as a key whose stored value is "". `load` is exported, so every caller is forced to treat a failed lookup as real data. `loadAll` (line 12) goes through `load`, so it also returns "" entries for missing keys and no longer fails when any key is absent. A caller that persists or acts on these values would use fabricated empty data without any signal.

findings.title: load() swallows missing-key error and returns empty string
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change, `load` threw `missing: <key>` when the key was absent. Now the throw sits inside a try block whose bare `catch` returns "". A missing key and a key legitimately stored as "" give the same result. This is an exported function, so every caller is forced to treat failure as a real value. `loadAll` (src/store.ts:12) maps over `load`, so it now silently returns "" entries for missing keys. Before, it threw on the first missing key. Callers can persist or use those empty values as real data, and nothing is logged.

findings.title: load() swallows missing-key error and returns empty string
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change, a missing key threw `missing: <key>`. The new try/catch catches that throw (and any other error, such as a null `store`) and returns "". `load` is exported, so every caller must now treat a failure the same as a real stored empty value. `loadAll` (src/store.ts:11-12) maps over `load`. findings.title: retryBackground discards final failure and deadline expiry silently
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported `retryBackground` returns void and has an empty `catch { continue; }`. When all `config.retries` attempts throw, it returns normally and the last error is lost. If the deadline passes first, it also returns normally. A caller cannot tell success from exhausted retries or a timeout, so it may treat a failed operation as done. The error is not logged either. Because the function is public, every caller is forced to conflate failure with success.

findings.title: Config rename breaks existing callers and silently disables the timeout
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported `Config.timeoutMs` is renamed to `timeout`, and a new required `retries` field is added. Existing callers passing `{maxAttempts, timeoutMs}` fail typechecking. Untyped or JS callers get `config.timeout === undefined`, so `deadline = Date.now() + undefined` is NaN. `Date.now() > NaN` is always false, so the deadline check never fires and the timeout is silently dropped. Callers of `retry` must now also supply `retries`, which `retry` never reads. `timeout` also no longer carries the unit that `timeoutMs` did.

findings.title: retryBackground swallows the final failure and reports success
findings.whyItBreaks: retryBackground is exported and returns void. Its catch block (lines 26-28) just `continue`s. When every attempt throws, or the deadline passes before any attempt succeeds, the function returns normally with no error and no result. A caller cannot tell 'fn succeeded' from 'all retries failed' or 'timed out before the first attempt'. Any caller that persists, bills or reports after the call will treat a failed job as done. The last error is dropped, so nothing can be logged or inspected either.

findings.title: Config rename drops unit and breaks existing callers silently
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported Config renames `timeoutMs` to `timeout`. It also adds a second required count field, `retries`, next to `maxAttempts`. Every existing caller of retry() must now supply both `timeout` and `retries`, even though retry() ignores `retries`. A JS or loosely typed caller that still passes `timeoutMs` gets `Date.now() + undefined = NaN`. `Date.now() > NaN` is always false, so the deadline is never enforced and the timeout guard is silently disabled. The new name `timeout` also loses the millisecond unit. The body treats it as ms, but a reader could assume seconds. No in-repo callers were found, but Config and retry are exported.

findings.title: Restore maxBuffer on git() so large PR diffs don't fail the run
findings.whyItBreaks: The git() helper previously set maxBuffer to 64MB. It now uses spawnSync's default of 1MB. runGithub() reads the full PR diff through this helper (`git diff mergeBase headSha`, line ~141), and changedFileSet() uses it too. Any PR whose diff output exceeds 1MB, such as a lockfile, generated code or vendored files, makes spawnSync kill the child and return an ENOBUFS error. In that case `res.status` is null, so the helper throws `git diff ... failed: ` with an empty message, because stderr is empty. These git calls run before the try/catch in runGithub, so the exception escapes. No 'Needlefish: review failed' check is posted, so a failure check never reaches the PR. The sibling gh()/ghText() helpers still keep the 64MB limit, so this looks like an unintended regression rather than a deliberate change.

findings.title: Restore maxBuffer on git() so large PR diffs don't hit ENOBUFS
findings.whyItBreaks: spawnSync without maxBuffer uses Node's default of 1 MiB. `git(['diff', mergeBase, headSha])` at line 140 returns the whole PR patch, and `git diff --name-only` at line 57 can also be large. A PR whose diff output exceeds 1 MiB (lockfiles, generated files, vendored code) makes spawnSync kill git with ENOBUFS. `res.status` is then null, so git() throws `git diff ... failed: ` with an empty message, because stderr is empty and the real error sits in `res.error`. Line 140 runs before the try/catch at line 176, so runGithub rejects without posting any check run. The PR gets no Needlefish result at all. The sibling helpers gh() and ghText() still set the 64MB buffer, which shows the large-output intent.

findings.title: Restore maxBuffer on git spawnSync; default 1MB breaks large PR diffs
findings.whyItBreaks: The git() helper previously passed maxBuffer of 64MB. Now it uses Node's spawnSync default of 1MB. runGithub() calls git(["diff", mergeBase, headSha]) to build the full patch. For any PR whose diff, or `git diff --name-only` output, exceeds 1MB, spawnSync kills the child and returns error=ENOBUFS with status null. `res.status !== 0` is then true, so git() throws `git diff ... failed: ` with an empty message, because stderr is empty. These git calls in runGithub (lines ~138-142) are outside the try/catch, so the exception escapes. No 'review failed' check run is posted, and the CI job crashes with an unhelpful error. gh() and ghText() in the same file still use the 64MB limit, so the git() helper was clearly meant to match them. This is a regression for large PRs such as lockfile or generated-file changes.

findings.title: Restore read-only sandbox for codex exec on untrusted repos
findings.whyItBreaks: runCodex spawns `codex exec` with cwd set to the repo under review and feeds it the diff and prompt, which is attacker-controllable text (prompt-injection surface). The removed `-s read-only` was the only thing forcing a read-only sandbox. Without it, codex uses whatever sandbox mode the user's ~/.codex/config.toml or profile sets. That can be workspace-write or danger-full-access, so an injected instruction could edit the repo, write files, or run mutating commands. This also contradicts the review contract that the agent only does read-only inspection. No other caller in the repo passes a sandbox flag, so nothing else compensates.

findings.title: Restore explicit read-only sandbox for codex exec
findings.whyItBreaks: `runCodex` is the only place the review agent's sandbox is set. It runs `codex exec` with `cwd: opts.repoPath`, the repo under review, and feeds it a prompt containing an untrusted diff. The old args pinned `-s read-only`. Without the flag, codex uses the sandbox from the user's config or profile, for example `sandbox_mode = workspace-write` or `danger-full-access`, or a config-level default. In that case a prompt-injection in the PR diff or repo files can make the agent write to the repo, run mutating commands, or reach outside it. That breaks the review agent's read-only guarantee. The change is silent: nothing in the code or in an option says the sandbox is now environment-dependent. I could not confirm the codex binary's built-in default from the repo, but even if it is read-only, the pin was what made this deterministic across user configs.

findings.title: Restore explicit read-only sandbox for codex exec
findings.whyItBreaks: The reviewer runs `codex exec` with cwd set to the repo under review. Its prompt includes untrusted diff and repo content. The old args pinned `-s read-only`, so a prompt-injected diff could not make the agent write files or run mutating commands. With the flag removed, the sandbox mode comes from the user's ~/.codex/config.toml or profile. A config with `sandbox_mode = "workspace-write"` or `danger-full-access`, which is common for interactive use, now applies to every review. The agent can then edit the reviewed repo, write outside it, or run arbitrary commands. The reviewer's read-only contract is no longer enforced by the code, and it varies silently by machine.

findings.title: Restore merge-base when diffing PR_BASE_SHA against the PR head
findings.whyItBreaks: The removed code ran `git merge-base baseSha headSha` and diffed from that merge base. The new code runs `git diff baseSha HEAD`, and `changedFileSet` runs `git diff --name-only baseSha HEAD` (line 57). When `PR_BASE_SHA` is set, it is normally the base-branch tip. In that case, if the PR branch has not been rebased onto the latest base, the two-dot diff also contains the inverse of every commit that landed on the base after the fork point. The reviewer then sees files and hunks the PR never touched. Those files enter `changedFiles` and `changedPaths`, which `postReview` uses to anchor inline comments (line 63). The result is false findings and misclassified surfaces. The code also now diffs against `HEAD` but reports `headSha`, which can come from `PR_HEAD_SHA`. If the checkout is the merge ref, `PR_HEAD_SHA` differs from `HEAD`. The patch and the SHA that review comments and check runs are posted to then describe different commits.

findings.title: Restore merge-base when diffing against PR_BASE_SHA
findings.whyItBreaks: `baseSha` comes from `PR_BASE_SHA` when it is set. In GitHub Actions that is normally the current base-branch tip (`pull_request.base.sha`), not the fork point. The removed `git merge-base baseSha headSha` step handled this case. `git diff <baseSha> HEAD` is a two-dot diff. If the base branch advanced after the PR branched, the patch and `changedFileSet` include the reverse of every commit that landed on the base branch since then, shown as deletions or reversions in files the PR never touched. The reviewer model gets a polluted patch and may report false findings on code the PR didn't change. `changedPaths` is also inflated, and `postReview` uses it in `inlineComments` to decide which findings get inline comments. The diff also uses `HEAD` where it previously used `headSha`. If `PR_HEAD_SHA` differs from the checked-out HEAD, such as a merge-ref checkout, the reviewed patch no longer matches the `headSha` that the review and check run are posted against.

findings.title: Restore merge-base diff; two-dot diff pulls in base-branch drift
findings.whyItBreaks: The patch and changed-file list are now `git diff baseSha HEAD`, where baseSha is `PR_BASE_SHA` (the base branch tip in Actions) or the `origin/main` merge-base fallback. When the base branch has advanced past the PR's fork point, a two-dot diff against the base tip also shows every upstream commit made since then, as reversed changes. The reviewer is then given the PR as having reverted unrelated files. It can raise false findings on code the PR never touched, and `changedPaths` (used to filter inline comments) and the changed-file surface classification are inflated. The old code computed `git merge-base baseSha headSha` first to avoid this. The diff also now uses the literal `HEAD` instead of `headSha`, while `bundle.headSha` and the check-run/review `commit_id` still use `PR_HEAD_SHA`. If the checkout is not exactly PR_HEAD_SHA (for example the synthetic merge ref), the reviewed patch no longer matches the SHA the results are posted against.

findings.title: Restore function replacers to avoid `$` pattern expansion in prompts
findings.whyItBreaks: String.prototype.replace treats a string replacement as a template. `$&`, `` $` ``, `$'`, `$$` and `$<name>` are expanded. The old `() => ...` form returned the text literally. `bundle.patch` is a raw diff of arbitrary code, so it routinely contains these sequences (shell/JS template code, regexes like `foo$'`, Makefiles, `$$` in YAML or shell). With the change, `$$` collapses to `$`, and `$&` is replaced by the matched `{{PATCH}}` placeholder. `` $` `` and `$'` inject the surrounding prompt text into the patch. The critic therefore sees a corrupted diff and can wrongly prune or confirm findings. The same applies to `JSON.stringify(candidate)` and the bundle at line 25, which embeds the diff, agentsMd and PR metadata. The failure is silent: nothing errors, the prompt is just altered.

findings.title: Restore function replacers to avoid `$` pattern corruption in prompts
findings.whyItBreaks: String.prototype.replace treats a string replacement specially: `$&`, `$'`, `` $` ``, `$$` and `$n` are expanded. The base code used `() => ...` to insert the text verbatim. This diff passes the raw strings `JSON.stringify(bundle)`, `JSON.stringify(candidate)` and `bundle.patch`. The bundle holds the full diff and repo AGENTS.md, and `bundle.patch` is the raw patch. Real code often contains these sequences, for example shell `$'...'`, `$&` in regex replacements, JS template/`$$` strings, or `$1` in sed and perl. Each one is silently rewritten: `$$` becomes `$`, `$&` becomes `{{BUNDLE}}`/`{{PATCH}}`, and `$'` or `` $` `` splice in the remainder or prefix of the prompt template. The reviewer and critic then see a corrupted diff and can produce wrong findings or miss real ones. The failure is silent. The affected code is the review input for exactly the kind of diff that contains these sequences.

findings.title: Restore function replacers to avoid `$` pattern expansion in prompts
findings.whyItBreaks: String.prototype.replace treats a string replacement as a pattern. `$&`, `$'`, `` $` ``, `$$` and `$1` are expanded. The diff changed all three replacements (`{{BUNDLE}}`, `{{FINDINGS}}`, `{{PATCH}}`) from `() => value` to the raw string. `bundle.patch` and the JSON-stringified bundle (which includes agentsMd and the diff) routinely contain such sequences, for example shell `$$` or `$'...'`, regex `$'`, and JS `$&`. `$$` collapses to `$`. `$'` and `` $` `` inject the text after or before the placeholder, which means a copy of the rest of the prompt template. The reviewer and critic then see a mutated or duplicated diff and prompt. That produces wrong or hallucinated findings, or wrongly pruned ones, for any PR touching code with these sequences. The function form returns the literal string without expansion, which is why it was there.

findings.title: Fallback review post drops commit_id pin to reviewed head SHA
findings.whyItBreaks: The primary path sends commit_id=headSha, but the fallback (taken when the primary POST throws, e.g. a 422 from an inline comment on a line outside the diff) no longer sends it. GitHub then attaches the review to the PR's current latest commit, not the SHA that was analysed. The review runs an LLM, so a push can land while it is in progress. In that case a REQUEST_CHANGES or COMMENT review based on the old diff gets attached to unreviewed new code. postCheck still reports against the old headSha, so the review and the check disagree. Before this change the fallback pinned the same SHA as the primary path, so the removal is a behavioural regression.

findings.title: Fallback review no longer pins commit_id to the reviewed SHA
findings.whyItBreaks: The primary POST sends commit_id=headSha (line 89), but the fallback now omits it. GitHub then attaches the review to the PR's current latest commit. The fallback runs on any primary failure. That includes a 422 caused by a stale or unknown commit_id after a push mid-run, or by an invalid inline comment position. In those cases the body-only review, built from a diff of the old headSha, is posted against the newer commit. A REQUEST_CHANGES review can then block a head that was never reviewed. Before this change the fallback shared the same pin, so a stale-SHA failure also failed the fallback instead of being silently re-targeted. postCheck still uses headSha (line 128), so the check run and the review can end up on different commits.

findings.title: normalizeFinding fabricates defaults instead of rejecting malformed findings
findings.whyItBreaks: The old code threw on an invalid severity or category, or on a missing file, title, whyItBreaks, suggestedFix or lineStart. It also threw when lineStart or lineEnd was non-finite or <= 0. The new code maps all of these to defaults. An invalid severity becomes "P1", which is a blocking-level severity the model never emitted. An invalid category becomes "bug". A missing title becomes "Untitled finding". A missing file becomes "". A missing lineStart becomes 0. Missing whyItBreaks and suggestedFix become "". A non-numeric lineStart such as "abc" becomes NaN, because Number() is not range-checked. Each of these values is a legitimate value of its type, so a caller cannot tell it from real data. `normalizeReview` calls this function for every finding at line 131. A garbled finding, such as `{}` or one with a bogus severity, now passes as a valid P1 finding with an empty file and line 0. It is then reported or used to decide the verdict. The old strict path would have failed the review. The old non-strict path would have dropped the bad finding. The `strict` flag and its drop-on-malformed mode are also removed entirely, so there is no way left to skip a malformed finding. Because `normalizeFinding` is exported, any other caller is forced to accept the same conflation. A null entry in `findings` still throws a raw TypeError from `raw.severity` instead of the old explicit 'not an object' error.

findings.title: normalizeFinding swallows validation errors and fabricates default findings
findings.whyItBreaks: The base version threw on an invalid severity or category, a missing file, title, whyItBreaks or suggestedFix, and a non-positive or non-finite lineStart or lineEnd. The head version maps every one of those to a default instead. An invalid severity becomes "P1", an invalid category becomes "bug", a missing file becomes "", lineStart and lineEnd become 0, and a missing title becomes "Untitled finding". whyItBreaks and suggestedFix become "". Non-numeric lineStart or lineEnd values such as "abc" become NaN, and a NaN confidence stays NaN because Math.max and Math.min propagate it. normalizeFinding and normalizeReview are exported and return the same Finding and RawReview types as before. A caller therefore cannot distinguish a garbage finding from a real P1 bug finding, and may report a fabricated P1 finding with no file or line. This also removes the old `strict=false` mode, which dropped malformed findings and kept the valid ones. `normalizeReview` now always maps every finding through the defaulting path. No in-repo callers were found, but the failure-to-default contract is itself the defect.

findings.title: normalizeFinding fabricates defaults for malformed findings instead of failing
findings.whyItBreaks: The removed code threw on an invalid severity or category, a missing file, title, whyItBreaks or suggestedFix, and a non-positive or non-finite lineStart or lineEnd. It also let normalizeReview drop bad findings when strict was false. The new code maps each of these failures to a plausible value: severity becomes "P1", category becomes "bug", the title becomes "Untitled finding", and file, whyItBreaks and suggestedFix become "". A missing lineStart becomes 0. A non-numeric lineStart such as "abc" becomes NaN and passes through. normalizeFinding and normalizeReview are exported, so callers can no longer tell a bad finding from a real one. A garbled finding with no severity is reported as a P1 with no file anchor and line 0. That can block a merge or post a bogus comment. The `strict` parameter was also removed, so a caller that wanted to skip malformed findings can no longer do so. A null or non-object element in `findings` still throws, but now as an incidental TypeError from reading `raw.severity` rather than the old explicit 'malformed finding' error.

findings.title: Restore explicit repo for gh pr view before checkout
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff drops `-R "$REPO"` and the `REPO` env var. The 'Resolve PR refs' step is the first step and runs before `actions/checkout`, so on a clean workspace there is no git remote for `gh` to infer the repo from. `GH_REPO` is also not set. In the workflow_dispatch branch (`EVENT_HEAD` empty), `gh pr view "$PR_NUM" --json ...` fails with a 'not a git repository' style error. The failure sits inside `$(...)` within `echo`, so the step still exits 0 and writes `head=` and `base=` as empty outputs. `actions/checkout` then runs with an empty `ref`, which falls back to the dispatching ref. `PR_HEAD_SHA` and `PR_BASE_SHA` are also empty in the review step. The manual run therefore reviews the wrong code or fails with an unclear error. It only works if a stale checkout happens to remain in the self-hosted runner workspace.

findings.title: Restore explicit repo for gh pr view before checkout
findings.whyItBreaks: The `Resolve PR refs` step is the first step in the job and runs before `actions/checkout`. For `workflow_dispatch`, `EVENT_HEAD` is empty, so the else branch runs `gh pr view "$PR_NUM" --json ...` with no `-R` and no `GH_REPO` env. `gh` then infers the repo from the current directory's git remotes. On a fresh or cleaned self-hosted workspace there is no git repo, so `gh` fails with 'not a git repository'. The failure happens inside `$(...)` within `echo`, so the step still exits 0 and writes empty `head=` and `base=` to `$GITHUB_OUTPUT`. The next step then runs `actions/checkout` with `ref: ''`, which checks out the default ref instead of the PR head. The review then runs against the wrong code with empty `PR_BASE_SHA` and `PR_HEAD_SHA`. A stale workspace from a previous run could also resolve the wrong repo.

findings.title: Restore repo selection for gh pr view before checkout
findings.whyItBreaks: The 'Resolve PR refs' step runs before actions/checkout, and the diff removes both `-R "$REPO"` and the `REPO` env var. `gh pr view` then has neither a flag nor GH_REPO, and it has no git remote to infer the repository from. On a clean workspace it fails with 'not a git repository'. The failure happens inside `$(...)` within `echo`, so the step still exits 0. It writes empty `head=` and `base=` outputs. `actions/checkout` with an empty `ref` checks out the default branch, not the PR head. `PR_HEAD_SHA` and `PR_BASE_SHA` are then empty in the review step. A manual workflow_dispatch run therefore fails or reviews the wrong code. A stale self-hosted workspace that happens to hold a repo would only hide the problem.

findings.title: normalizeReview fails open on malformed review output
findings.whyItBreaks: The base version threw "malformed review output: ..." when raw was not an object, or when summary, findings, checked or residual_risks were missing or the wrong type. The new code maps every one of those cases to a default: findings [], residual_risks [], checked [], summary "". An agent reply that is null, truncated, or has `findings` as a string or object now normalizes to {summary:"", findings:[], checked:[], residual_risks:[]}. That result cannot be told apart from a real clean review that found nothing. Any caller that derives a Verdict (`pass | changes_requested | needs_human`) from findings and residual_risks will see no findings and no blocking risks, so it can report `pass`. The function is exported, so every caller is forced to treat failure as a valid value. A `findings` field that is present but not an array has its entire contents silently dropped, so real P0/P1 findings can be lost.

findings.title: normalizeReview swallows malformed output into an empty clean review
findings.whyItBreaks: The old code threw "malformed review output: ..." when raw was not an object, or when summary, findings, checked or residual_risks were missing or the wrong type. Now null, a string, `{}`, or a response that dropped `findings` or `residual_risks` all become `{summary:"", findings:[], checked:[], residual_risks:[]}`. That has the same shape as a legitimate zero-finding review, with no blocking residual risks. The exported function now forces every caller to treat "the reviewer failed or returned garbage" as "nothing found". A verdict derived from findings and blocking risks would then come out as `pass` on a truncated or non-JSON model response. A missing `residual_risks` array also silently discards any blocking risks the reviewer reported. Verified by reading: the repo has no in-repo caller and no verdict computation yet, so this is the public API contract defect rather than an observed bad call path.

findings.title: Malformed review output is silently normalized into an empty clean review
findings.whyItBreaks: The base version threw `malformed review output: ...` when raw was not an object, or when summary, findings, checked or residual_risks had the wrong type or was missing. The new code maps each of those failures to a default: `findings` becomes [], `residual_risks` becomes [], `checked` becomes [] and `summary` becomes "". A truncated or garbage model response, `null`, a plain string, or output with a misspelled key (for example `finding` or `residualRisks`) now returns a valid RawReview with zero findings and zero blocking residual risks. A verdict derived from that is indistinguishable from a real PASS. The same applies if the model emitted real findings under a wrong key: they are dropped and the result still looks clean. normalizeReview is exported, so every caller is forced to treat failure as a legitimate empty review, and the old error is no longer available to retry or fail the run. The old error text now appears nowhere in the repo.

findings.title: workflow_dispatch no longer checks out or passes the PR's head/base
findings.whyItBreaks: The removed 'Resolve PR refs' step was the only place the workflow_dispatch case (manual `pr_number` input) mapped a PR number to head/base SHAs via `gh pr view`. The job `if` at line 24 still allows `workflow_dispatch`. On dispatch, `github.event.pull_request` is empty, so: (1) checkout `ref` falls back to `github.ref`, the branch the workflow was dispatched from (usually main), not the PR head. Because this is the self-review setup, `src/cli.ts` and the working tree are then the wrong code. (2) The base fetch silently uses the hard-coded `main`, which is wrong for PRs targeting other branches. (3) `PR_BASE_SHA` and `PR_HEAD_SHA` are exported as empty strings, so the CLI gets no explicit SHAs for the PR it is told to review. The manual trigger therefore reviews or diffs the wrong tree, or fails, with no error at the workflow level.

findings.title: workflow_dispatch review no longer resolves the PR's head/base
findings.whyItBreaks: The workflow still advertises manual dispatch through the `pr_number` input and the job `if`. The removed `Resolve PR refs` step looked up head and base from `gh pr view "$PR_NUM"` when no `pull_request` payload existed. The new code reads everything from `github.event.pull_request.*`, which is empty on `workflow_dispatch`. (1) Checkout `ref` falls back to `github.ref`, the branch the workflow was dispatched on (usually main), not the PR head, so the PR code is not checked out. (2) `BASE_REF` falls back to `'main'` even when the PR targets another branch. (3) `PR_BASE_SHA` and `PR_HEAD_SHA` are exported as empty strings, so the CLI gets no explicit SHAs. A manual run therefore reviews the wrong tree or diff range, or fails, unless the CLI independently re-resolves the SHAs. I could not confirm that: `src/cli.ts` is not in this checkout, which contains only the workflow and `.needlefish/answers.json`.

findings.title: workflow_dispatch no longer resolves PR head/base; reviews wrong ref
findings.whyItBreaks: The deleted 'Resolve PR refs' step used `gh pr view $PR_NUM` to fill head/base SHAs when the event had no pull_request payload, which is the workflow_dispatch case (still offered, with a required `pr_number` input, at lines 10-14). Now `github.event.pull_request.head.sha` is empty on dispatch, so checkout falls back to `github.ref`, the branch the run was dispatched from (usually main) and not the PR head. The 'Fetch base branch' step hardcodes `main`. `PR_BASE_SHA` and `PR_HEAD_SHA` (lines 45-46) are exported as empty strings, where before they held the resolved SHAs. A manual review of PR N therefore runs against main's tree with no SHAs, so the review is empty, reviews the wrong code, or fails. In this self-review setup the tool source is the checkout's `src/`, so the wrong code is also run as the tool. The base ref is also wrong for PRs that target a non-main branch.

findings.title: Restore maxBuffer for git() so large diffs don't fail with ENOBUFS
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff drops `maxBuffer: 1024 * 1024 * 64`, so Node's spawnSync default of 1 MiB applies. `git diff baseSha HEAD` at line 100 produces the full patch, which easily exceeds 1 MiB on large PRs (lockfiles, generated code, vendored files). Past the limit spawnSync kills the child and sets `res.error` (ENOBUFS), and `res.status` is null. The `status !== 0` check then throws `git diff ... failed: ` with an empty stderr, so the review aborts with no useful message. The sibling `gh()` helper still sets 64 MiB, so this also makes the two helpers inconsistent. Nothing else in the diff justifies the removal.

findings.title: Restore maxBuffer on git() so large diffs don't fail with ENOBUFS
findings.whyItBreaks: The change removed `maxBuffer: 64MB`, so `spawnSync` falls back to Node's 1 MiB default. The same helper runs `git diff <base> HEAD` at line 100 to build the full review patch. Any diff over 1 MiB now makes spawnSync kill git and return `status === null` with `res.error = ENOBUFS`. The `status !== 0` check then throws `git diff ... failed: ` with an empty stderr, so the real cause is hidden. Reviews of large branches, such as lockfile or generated-file changes, worked before and now abort. The sibling `gh()` helper at line 36 still sets the 64MB cap, so the two helpers are now inconsistent.

findings.title: Restore maxBuffer so large git diffs don't fail with ENOBUFS
findings.whyItBreaks: The change drops `maxBuffer: 64MB` from `spawnSync`. Node's default maxBuffer for spawnSync is 1MB. `git diff baseSha HEAD` (line 100) can easily exceed 1MB on a large PR, lockfile change or generated files. In that case spawnSync kills the child and returns `status === null` with `error=ENOBUFS`. The check `res.status !== 0` then throws `git diff ... failed: ` with an empty stderr, and the real cause (ENOBUFS) is never shown. The local review therefore fails on exactly the large diffs where it is most needed. Small diffs still work, so the regression is easy to miss.

findings.title: Errored review must not report a neutral check conclusion
findings.whyItBreaks: The catch path now posts conclusion "neutral" instead of "failure". GitHub treats a neutral check as passing for required status checks, so a crashed, timed-out or misconfigured review no longer blocks merge. The summary text still says "did NOT pass this PR", which contradicts the conclusion. The exit code is still 1, but branch protection reads the check-run conclusion, not the job's exit code. The previous behavior was deliberately fail-closed.

findings.title: gh pr diff is fetched outside the try block and can fail or diverge
findings.whyItBreaks: The patch used to come from the local `git diff baseSha HEAD`. It now comes from `gh pr diff`, which is called with no `cwd` and sits outside the try/catch that posts the failure check. `gh pr diff` can fail where local git does not: the GitHub API rejects very large diffs (HTTP 406, over 20000 lines), and the call needs a repo context from the process cwd or `GH_REPO`. When it throws, `runGithub` rejects before any check run is posted, so a large PR gets no Needlefish check at all. The patch now contains only the PR's own changes, while `changedFiles` and `changedPaths` still come from the local `git diff baseSha HEAD`. These can disagree when the checkout is not the merge commit or the base has moved. The model can then be shown a different file set than the one used to anchor inline comments.

findings.title: Untrusted PR head is now installed and executed as the review tool
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change the tool (`needlefish`) came from `frankekn/needlefish@main` and the PR head was only checked out as data under `target/`. After it, the PR head is checked out at the workspace root, `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` runs with the PR's package.json, lockfile and lifecycle scripts, and `./node_modules/.bin/tsx src/cli.ts` runs the PR's own src/. The job's `if` (line 24) only blocks fork PRs for the `pull_request` event. `workflow_dispatch` passes unconditionally, and `pr_number` is free-form and resolved via `gh pr view` (lines 31-41). A dispatch against a fork PR therefore checks out fork-controlled head SHA and runs its install scripts and CLI on a `self-hosted` runner. That step has `GH_TOKEN` with `pull-requests: write` and `checks: write`, and the runner uses a login zsh with a persistent environment. Same-repo `pull_request` runs were already exposed through the PR's modified workflow file, so the new exposure is the dispatch-on-fork-PR path. It also removes the stated protection that a PR cannot control its own review.

findings.title: Severity normalization removed; 'p0'/' P1 ' now silently downgrade to P3
findings.whyItBreaks: The base code did `String(raw.severity ?? "").trim().toUpperCase()` before checking `SEVERITIES`. So model output such as "p0", "p1" or "P1 " mapped to the correct severity. The new code runs `SEVERITIES.includes(raw.severity)` on the raw value, which is case-sensitive and does not trim. Any non-canonical spelling of a blocking severity now falls through to the default. The default was also lowered from P1 to P3, so a critical finding reported as "p0" becomes a P3 with no error or log. Severity drives how serious a finding looks and, presumably, the `Verdict` in `ReviewResult`. A merge-blocking issue can therefore be reported as low-risk. Failure to parse severity is mapped to a default, and callers cannot tell that apart from a real P3. A missing or invalid severity is also now treated as non-blocking, where the old default was P1.

findings.title: Severity normalization regression downgrades p0/p1 findings to P3
findings.whyItBreaks: The old code did String(raw.severity).trim().toUpperCase() before the SEVERITIES check, so 'p0', 'P1 ' and 'p2' were accepted. The new code checks raw.severity verbatim. Any case or whitespace variant now fails the check, and the fallback was also lowered from P1 to P3. For example, a model-emitted {severity:'p0'} used to become P0 and now becomes P3 with no error or log. The input comes from LLM JSON via normalizeReview (src/shared/schema.ts:132), where casing drift is common. A critical finding can be shown as low-severity, and any severity-based verdict or gating that sits downstream would not block on it. A missing or invalid severity also used to fail safe at P1 and now fails open at P3. normalizeFinding is exported, so every caller gets this conflation of 'invalid severity' with a real P3.

findings.title: Severity normalization removed; invalid or lowercase severities downgrade to P3
findings.whyItBreaks: The old code did String(raw.severity).trim().toUpperCase() before checking SEVERITIES, so "p0", "p1" and " P2 " were accepted. The new code runs SEVERITIES.includes(raw.severity) on the raw value. Any case or whitespace variant now fails the check and falls through to the default, which was also changed from "P1" to "P3". A model-emitted "p0" security finding is therefore reported as P3, the lowest and non-blocking tier. A missing or garbage severity also used to fail safe at P1 and now becomes P3. This is a silent downgrade of an unparseable severity signal into a plausible-looking valid value. normalizeReview applies it to every finding (schema.ts:132), so the downgrade affects all findings in a review.

findings.title: Restore GitHub token scrubbing for the spawned codex process
findings.whyItBreaks: The base code built a copy of process.env with GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN and GITHUB_API_TOKEN deleted, and passed it to spawnSync. The change drops that copy and the `env` option, so the child inherits the full parent environment. `codex exec` runs with the repo under review as its cwd and prompt, which is untrusted PR content. A prompt-injected diff or repo file can therefore get the model to run a read-only shell command that dumps the env, such as `env` or `printenv`, and leak the GitHub credentials. The read-only sandbox restricts file writes, not env inspection. Codex's own default env filter is a weaker, configuration-dependent defense, and it does not cover every token name. Nothing in the diff or repo explains why the hardening was removed.

findings.title: Restore GitHub token scrubbing from codex subprocess env
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff deletes the env copy that removed GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN and GITHUB_API_TOKEN, and removes `env` from the spawnSync options. The codex child now inherits the full process.env, including any GitHub credentials the caller has. That child is an LLM agent. It reads untrusted diff and repo content and can run shell commands even under `-s read-only`. A prompt injection in a reviewed PR can therefore make it read the tokens (for example by running `env`). The tokens can then be leaked through its output, which is returned and possibly posted, or through network calls if the sandbox allows them. The removed code was an explicit credential-isolation control. Nothing in the diff replaces it, and the review has no need for GitHub credentials.

findings.title: Restore GitHub token scrubbing for the codex subprocess env
findings.whyItBreaks: The removed lines deleted GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN and GITHUB_API_TOKEN from the env before spawning `codex exec`. Without an explicit `env`, spawnSync inherits the full process.env, so those tokens now reach the model agent. That agent runs with the repo as cwd and a prompt containing untrusted PR diff content, so a prompt-injected diff could make it read the tokens, for example by running `env` or `printenv` in its shell tool. It could then leak them through the last message, which is returned to the caller and likely posted or logged. `-s read-only` limits writes. It does not hide the process environment. This reverses a deliberate hardening step with no replacement.

findings.title: Restore fork guard before running PR code on self-hosted runner
findings.whyItBreaks: The job runs on `runs-on: self-hosted` and is triggered by `pull_request`. The `if: head.repo.full_name == github.repository` guard is removed, so PRs from forks now run the job too. The job checks out the fork's head SHA. It then runs `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile`, which executes lifecycle scripts from the PR's package.json and dependencies. It then runs `./node_modules/.bin/tsx src/cli.ts` from the PR's own source. A fork author can open a PR that changes `src/` or the install scripts and get arbitrary code execution on Frank's self-hosted machine. That machine runs a login zsh shell, so it likely has user credentials and local state. GitHub's fork-PR read-only token does not protect the runner itself. Fork PRs may need approval first, but that is a repo setting, not something this workflow enforces. The workflow's own comment says it is self-review mode, where the PR checkout is the tool. That makes executing PR-controlled code intentional, which is why the guard was the only barrier.

findings.title: Restore fork guard: fork PR code runs on self-hosted runner
findings.whyItBreaks: The deleted `if: github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name == github.repository` was the only thing stopping fork PRs from running this job. The job is on `pull_request`, uses `runs-on: self-hosted`, and checks out `github.event.pull_request.head.sha`. It then runs `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` and `./node_modules/.bin/tsx src/cli.ts` from that checkout. Without the guard, anyone who can open a fork PR can run arbitrary code on Frank's machine. A modified `package.json` lifecycle script, a modified lockfile source, or a modified `src/cli.ts` would each do it. The fork-PR token is read-only and has no secrets, but that does not contain code execution on a persistent self-hosted host. The host can still expose the local network, the filesystem, the zsh login environment and credentials, and persistence for later jobs. Public repositories should not use self-hosted runners for untrusted PRs.

findings.title: Restore fork guard on self-hosted runner executing PR code
findings.whyItBreaks: The deleted `if: github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name == github.repository` was the only thing keeping fork PRs off this job. The job runs on `runs-on: self-hosted`. It checks out `github.event.pull_request.head.sha`, then runs `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` and `./node_modules/.bin/tsx src/cli.ts` from that checkout. Anyone who opens a PR from a fork can now change package.json, the lockfile, install scripts or src/cli.ts. Their code then executes on Frank's own machine inside a login zsh shell (`zsh -l`), with that user's environment and files. For fork PRs GitHub usually gives a read-only token and withholds secrets. findings.title: Zero runner duration env override is now silently replaced by default
findings.whyItBreaks: Changing `parsed >= 0` to `parsed > 0` makes `readRunnerDurationMs` treat `0` as invalid and return `fallbackMs`. `NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS=0` used to mean 'SIGKILL immediately after SIGTERM'. It now silently becomes 5000 ms. `NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS=0` used to mean 'stop waiting for close right after SIGKILL'. It now silently becomes 2000 ms. The function is exported and its callers at lines 3-10 pass the values straight to `setTimeout` at lines 118-124. A user who explicitly set 0 gets no error or warning, only much longer hangs on timed-out runners. A valid value is treated as invalid and defaulted, so a configured 0 can't be told apart from an unset variable. Nothing else in the repo (no docs or tests) says 0 is meant to be rejected.

findings.title: Explicit 0 for runner grace/give-up env vars is now silently ignored
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change, NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS=0 and NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS=0 were accepted (parsed >= 0). They meant SIGKILL immediately after SIGTERM, and stop waiting for 'close' immediately after SIGKILL. With `> 0`, an explicit "0" is now silently replaced by the defaults of 5000ms and 2000ms. Nothing is logged. Anyone who relied on 0, for example CI or tests wanting fast escalation, now waits up to 7s longer per timed-out runner with no signal that their setting was dropped. setTimeout(fn, 0) is valid for both consumers at lines 118-124. If rejecting 0 is intentional, the change should be documented.

findings.title: Deep-pass residual risks are discarded, so blocking gaps can't affect the verdict
findings.whyItBreaks: The loop now reads only `res.findings` and `res.summary` from each deep pass. `res.residual_risks` is never collected, and `candidateMerged.residual_risks` is hard-coded to `[]`. The critic therefore never sees the deep passes' unresolved or blocking risks. `deriveVerdict(pruned.findings, pruned.residual_risks)` at line 122 reads only the critic's residuals. Base code accumulated them with `residuals.push(...res.residual_risks)` and passed them into the critic input. Now a deep pass that reports `blocks:true` (for example 'could not verify guard X') leaves no trace in the result. When the critic also reports no findings, the verdict can be PASS. This is a swallowed failure signal (TRIGGER D). Previously the signal reached the critic input at the old line `residual_risks: residuals`. Now the critic receives `[]`, so it cannot be distinguished from 'no risks'.

findings.title: Removed coverage backstop lets changed files skip deep review with no signal
findings.whyItBreaks: Only the top `MAX_HOTSPOTS` (6) hotspots are deep-reviewed. Any changed file the map pass omitted, or any file in a hotspot cut by `.slice(0, MAX_HOTSPOTS)`, is never reviewed. The removed block added a tail hotspot for every uncovered file. Nothing replaces it, not even a residual risk. Large PRs have more than 10 files by definition, so this path is hit exactly when the map is most likely to miss files. The final result can be PASS or a clean review for code that was never read. The same removal covers the per-hotspot try/catch residual with `blocks:true`. A deep-pass failure now throws and aborts the whole review, discarding the findings already gathered from earlier hotspots.

findings.title: Restore coverage backstop so unmapped changed files are still reviewed
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff deletes the tail-coverage hotspot. reviewLarge now deep-reviews only `sortByRisk(mapResult.hotspots).slice(0, MAX_HOTSPOTS)`. MAX_HOTSPOTS is 6 (line 26). Any changed file that the map pass assigned to no hotspot, or that sits in a hotspot dropped by the slice, is never read by a deep pass. Nothing records that it was skipped: no residual risk is emitted and the critic is only given patchStat. A large PR (more than 10 files or more than 30000 chars) can therefore pass with whole files unreviewed. The deleted code existed to prevent exactly this ('never silently skip a changed file').

findings.title: Preserve deep-pass residual_risks instead of discarding them
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously each deep pass's `res.residual_risks` was collected into `residuals`, and a failed deep pass was recorded as a blocks=true residual. That list went into candidateMerged and the critic. Now `res.residual_risks` is never read (lines 103-105) and candidateMerged hard-codes `residual_risks: []` (line 113). Blocking evidence gaps from deep passes (for example 'could not verify X', unresolved sentinel tracing) never reach the critic. The final verdict comes from `deriveVerdict(pruned.findings, pruned.residual_risks)` (line 122), so the verdict only reflects residual risks the critic re-invents. A deep pass that reports blocks=true can therefore yield PASS. The signal reached `residuals` (and so the critic and the verdict) before the change. Now it goes nowhere.

findings.title: Restore coverage backstop for files outside the top MAX_HOTSPOTS hotspots
findings.whyItBreaks: The hotspots are sorted and cut to MAX_HOTSPOTS (6). The removed tail-coverage hotspot was the only thing that sent changed files outside those hotspots, or files the map pass never assigned, to a deep review. Now any such file is never deep-reviewed. Nothing records that it was skipped, so the critic and deriveVerdict can return PASS without ever looking at it. The removed comment said 'never silently skip a changed file'; this reintroduces exactly that.

findings.title: Propagate deep-pass residual_risks into the critic input and final result
findings.whyItBreaks: Each deep pass returns res.residual_risks, including blocks=true entries for evidence gaps. These are no longer collected. candidateMerged hard-codes residual_risks: [], and the final result uses pruned.residual_risks, which comes only from the critic. The critic is given neither the deep-pass residuals nor the original patch, so it cannot reconstruct them. deriveVerdict(pruned.findings, pruned.residual_risks) at line 122 will therefore return PASS where a blocking residual risk would previously have blocked it. That is a silent loss of the signal that gates the verdict.

findings.title: Large-PR review silently drops user focus/deep options
findings.whyItBreaks: The base code threaded `bundle.focus` into the deep prompt via `{{FOCUS}}` and passed `focus` and `deep` in `mapBundle`. The diff removes all three. `reviewSmall` still sends the full bundle, which includes `focus` and `deep`. So a run with a focus or deep option is honored on small PRs and ignored on large PRs, with no warning. If `prompts/deep.md` still contains `{{FOCUS}}`, the unreplaced literal now goes to the model. The prompts directory is not in this repo snapshot, so that part is unverified. The `focus` and `deep` fields are still on `Bundle`, which suggests the removal is not an intentional feature drop.

findings.title: Large-PR path silently drops focus/deep review options
findings.whyItBreaks: `Bundle` carries `focus` and `deep`. `reviewSmall` still sends the whole bundle to review.md, so both options apply there. This diff removes them from `mapBundle` (map.md input) and removes the `{{FOCUS}}` substitution from the deep.md prompt in `reviewLarge`. Any PR with a patch over 30000 chars or more than 10 files now ignores the user's focus instruction and the deep flag, with no error or warning. The same invocation therefore behaves differently depending on PR size. The map pass also can't rank hotspots by the requested focus. The prompts directory isn't in this snapshot, so I couldn't check whether deep.md still contains a `{{FOCUS}}` token. If it does, the model receives the literal text `{{FOCUS}}` instead of a value.

findings.title: Large-PR path silently drops user-supplied focus/deep options
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff removes `focus` and `deep` from `mapBundle` in `reviewLarge`. It also removes the `{{FOCUS}}` substitution from the `deep.md` prompt build. The small path (`reviewSmall`, ~line 52) still serialises the whole bundle, including `focus` and `deep`, into `review.md`. A user who runs with a focus or deep option therefore gets it honored on small PRs and ignored on large ones. No warning or residual risk is emitted. The map pass can no longer weight hotspots by focus, and the per-hotspot deep reviews lose the focus instruction. If `prompts/deep.md` still contains the `{{FOCUS}}` placeholder, it will now reach the model as literal text because nothing replaces it. `prompts/` is not in this checkout, so I could not confirm that.

findings.title: formatDuration emits '60s' / 'Nm 60s' near minute boundaries
findings.whyItBreaks: Minutes are floored from raw ms, then seconds are rounded separately. When ms % 60000 >= 59500, the seconds value rounds up to 60 but minutes is not incremented. ms=59600 gives minutes=0, seconds=Math.round(59.6)=60, so the output is '60s'. The old code rounded to total seconds first (60) and printed '1m 0s'. ms=119700 gives '1m 60s', where the old code gave '2m 0s'. This is a regression introduced by the reorder. The output appears in the user-facing stats line at render.ts:75 and render.ts:80.

findings.title: formatDuration can emit 60 seconds instead of rolling over to the minute
findings.whyItBreaks: The new code floors the minutes from raw ms but rounds the seconds remainder separately. When ms % 60000 >= 59500, Math.round gives 60 and the minutes value is not incremented. For example, 59500ms renders "60s" instead of "1m 0s", and 119600ms renders "1m 60s" instead of "2m 0s". The old code rounded to total seconds first, so seconds % 60 was always 0..59. Both the per-step durations (render.ts:75) and the total (render.ts:80) use this function.

findings.title: formatDuration emits 60 seconds instead of carrying into minutes
findings.whyItBreaks: Minutes are floored from the raw ms, but seconds are rounded separately from the remainder. Any remainder of 59500..59999 ms rounds to 60 with no carry into minutes. Examples: 119500 ms gives "1m 60s" (the old code gave "2m 0s"). 59500 ms gives "60s" (the old code gave "1m 0s"). The function is used for the per-step and total durations in the rendered markdown (render.ts:75, 80), so the review output shows invalid times.

findings.title: parsePositiveInteger now accepts 0 despite promising a positive integer
findings.whyItBreaks: The guard changed from `parsed <= 0` to `parsed < 0`, so `parsePositiveInteger("0", label)` now returns 0 instead of throwing. The exported name and the error text on line 33 (`requires a positive integer`) both promise a value greater than zero. Any caller that uses it for a timeout, retry count, concurrency, or similar option (RunnerOptions.timeoutMs is the obvious fit) now silently gets 0. That can mean an immediate timeout, zero attempts, or an infinite or disabled limit, depending on the consumer. A user who passes 0 also no longer gets the validation error. No in-repo caller exists, but the function is public, and the promise it makes about the returned value is the contract.

findings.title: parsePositiveInteger now accepts 0, empty and blank strings
findings.whyItBreaks: The function is exported and named parsePositiveInteger, and its error text says 'requires a positive integer'. The change from `parsed <= 0` to `parsed < 0` lets 0 and -0 through. Because `Number("")` and `Number("   ")` both evaluate to 0, an empty or blank value, such as an unset or empty CLI flag or env var, is now silently accepted as 0. Before this change the `<= 0` check rejected all of these. Any caller using this for timeouts, counts or retries would receive 0 (a zero timeout, zero attempts or an immediate abort) instead of an error. The error message still says 'positive' for a check that no longer enforces it.

findings.title: parsePositiveInteger now accepts 0 and empty input
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported function is named `parsePositiveInteger` and throws "requires a positive integer". The guard changed from `parsed <= 0` to `parsed < 0`, so 0 is now returned as valid. `Number("")` and `Number("   ")` are also 0, so empty or whitespace-only input, previously rejected, now silently parses to 0. A caller that parses a timeout, count or retry value (for example `RunnerOptions.timeoutMs`) gets 0 where it expects at least 1. Depending on how the value is used, that means an immediate timeout, zero attempts, or a disabled limit. The body no longer matches the name or the error text.
